questions.stem: In the Indian Constitution, the power to amend the Constitution and its procedures is laid down in which Article?

options.option_text: Article 368
Article 370
Article 356
Article 123

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Article 368 (Part XX) deals with the powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure. It allows Parliament to add, vary, or repeal any provision of the Constitution.
DECOY BUSTING: Article 370 dealt with the special status of Jammu & Kashmir (abrogated in 2019). Article 356 deals with President's Rule. Article 123 deals with Presidential Ordinances.
EXAM INSIGHT: Crucially, in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that while Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution under Art 368, it CANNOT destroy or alter its 'Basic Structure'.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under which Article of the Constitution does Parliament derive its power and the procedure to amend the Constitution?

options.option_text: Article 352, governing proclamation of national emergency
Article 356, governing imposition of President's Rule in states
Article 368, governing power and procedure to amend the Constitution
Article 370, governing special status of Jammu and Kashmir

questions.explanation: Article 368 in Part XX is titled 'Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor.' It vests both the authority and the procedural requirements in Parliament. Articles 352 and 356 deal with emergency provisions; Article 370 (now abrogated) dealt with J&K's special status — none govern the amendment procedure.

questions.stem: A constitutional amendment bill under Article 368 requires a 'special majority.' Which option correctly defines this special majority?

options.option_text: A bare majority of the total membership of each House of Parliament only
Two-thirds of members present and voting in each House, with no other condition
Total membership majority AND two-thirds of those present and voting in each House
Three-fourths of total membership in a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament

questions.explanation: Article 368(2) requires BOTH conditions in each House: (i) a majority of the total membership of that House, AND (ii) at least two-thirds of the members present and voting. Option A omits the two-thirds limb; Option B omits the total-membership limb. Option D is wrong because no provision for a joint session exists for constitutional amendments — this is a common distractor drawn from the ordinary legislative deadlock mechanism.

questions.stem: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 inserted the Ninth Schedule into the Constitution. What was the primary purpose of shielding laws under this Schedule?

options.option_text: Protecting nationalization of banks and industries from Right to Equality challenges
Protecting land reform and zamindari abolition laws from Right to Property challenges
Protecting reservation laws for OBCs from Fundamental Rights challenges
Protecting press regulation laws from freedom of speech challenges in courts

questions.explanation: The Ninth Schedule was created specifically to protect state land reform and zamindari abolition laws that courts were striking down as violations of the Right to Property (then protected under Articles 19 and 31). Bank nationalisation came much later (1969) and was a separate controversy. OBC reservation (Mandal) was a 1990s issue. Press regulation was addressed separately by amending Article 19(2) — not the primary reason for the Ninth Schedule.

questions.stem: Which constitutional amendment act incorporated Fundamental Duties into the Constitution, acting on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee?

options.option_text: 44th Amendment Act, 1978 — which reversed many earlier changes
42nd Amendment Act, 1976 — which inserted Part IVA into the Constitution
86th Amendment Act, 2002 — which made education a fundamental right
73rd Amendment Act, 1992 — which gave constitutional status to panchayats

questions.explanation: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended adding Fundamental Duties. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Article 51A under new Part IVA, listing 10 duties. The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed several other provisions of the 42nd Amendment but left Fundamental Duties intact. The 86th Amendment (2002) added only one new duty — Article 51A(k) on parental responsibility for a child's education — it did not create Part IVA.

questions.stem: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 is often called the 'Mini-Constitution.' Which of the following changes is NOT attributable to this amendment?

options.option_text: Transfer of Education and Forests from State List to Concurrent List
Reduction of the voting age from 21 to 18 years for Lok Sabha elections
Addition of 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble of the Constitution
Curtailment of the power of courts to judicially review constitutional amendments

questions.explanation: The reduction of voting age from 21 to 18 was effected by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 — not the 42nd Amendment. The 42nd Amendment did: transfer five subjects (Education, Forests, Weights & Measures, Wild Animals, Administration of Justice) to the Concurrent List; add 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble; and insert Articles 368(4)–(5) to insulate amendments from judicial review (later struck down in Minerva Mills, 1980).

questions.stem: Which of the following parliamentary actions does NOT require the special majority procedure under Article 368 and can be accomplished by a simple majority in Parliament?

options.option_text: Amending provisions related to the election of the President of India
Forming a new state or altering the boundary of an existing state
Amending provisions related to the organisation of the Union Judiciary
Amending provisions related to representation of states in Parliament

questions.explanation: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new states, alter boundaries, change names, etc. through an ordinary bill passed by simple majority (with Presidential recommendation) — it is explicitly outside Article 368. In contrast, provisions on Presidential election (Articles 54–55), Union Judiciary (Articles 124–147), and representation of states in Parliament are listed in Article 368(2) proviso as requiring special majority PLUS ratification by at least half the state legislatures. A common error is assuming all constitutional text changes must go through Article 368.

questions.stem: The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) established the Basic Structure doctrine. Which of the following has been consistently upheld as part of 'Basic Structure' in subsequent landmark judgments?

options.option_text: The right to hold property as a constitutional guarantee under Article 300A
Judicial review and the independence of the judiciary from executive control
The specific directive principles listed under Articles 39 to 51 of the Constitution
Parliamentary privileges and the immunity of legislators under Article 105

questions.explanation: Judicial review and independence of the judiciary have been affirmed as core Basic Structure elements in S.P. Gupta (1981) and emphatically reaffirmed in the NJAC judgment (2015), where the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment precisely on this ground. The right to property was removed as a Fundamental Right by the 44th Amendment and reduced to a statutory right under Article 300A — it has not been recognised as Basic Structure. The DPSPs in their specific textual form are not Basic Structure; only their underlying constitutional 'essence' receives protection. Parliamentary privilege is significant but has never been held to be Basic Structure.
